summary.text: Statistical mechanics applies probability and statistics to huge numbers of microscopic particles to explain the properties of matter in bulk.
It explains temperature, pressure and heat capacity from microscopic behaviour, and it bridges exact mechanics and our incomplete knowledge by using an ensemble of possible states.
Maxwell's 1859 velocity distribution was the first statistical law in physics, Boltzmann built the field from the 1870s, and Gibbs formalized it in 1902.

facts.label: Boltzmann's start
facts.value: The field began in the 1870s with his work

facts.label: Statistical ensemble
facts.value: Many virtual copies of a system in various states

facts.label: Bernoulli's insight
facts.value: Gas pressure comes from molecules hitting a surface

items.prompt: A scientist wants the pressure of a room's air, which holds countless molecules. Why does she not simply track each one?

options.label: Air molecules hold perfectly still
Each one is unneeded, and cannot be known exactly
Pressure has nothing to do with molecules
Molecules exist only as a mathematical idea

items.explain: Everyday life does not require, and quantum mechanics does not allow, knowing every particle's exact position and momentum, so uncertainty about the state is added.

items.prompt: A physicist imagines a huge number of imaginary copies of one box of gas, each in a different microscopic state. What does this collection represent?

options.label: A probability distribution over the possible states
A list of every real gas box in the world
The one exact state the gas is in
A record of how the gas changed over time

items.explain: The statistical ensemble is a large collection of virtual copies in various states, serving as a probability distribution over all possible states.

items.prompt: Why does a balloon feel firm when you squeeze it, according to Bernoulli's picture of gases?

options.label: The gas is a solid jelly
The gas particles stick to the walls
Heat flows out through the rubber
Countless molecules keep hitting the surface

items.explain: Bernoulli argued that gases are great numbers of molecules moving in all directions, and their impacts on a surface cause the pressure we feel.

items.prompt: A chemist wants to model how fast a reaction proceeds, not only the final balance it reaches. Which part of the field helps?

options.label: Classical thermodynamics of equilibrium alone
Counting molecules by hand
Non-equilibrium statistical mechanics
The ensemble of a single particle

items.explain: Classical thermodynamics deals mainly with equilibrium, while non-equilibrium statistical mechanics models the speed of irreversible processes such as chemical reactions.

items.prompt: Gibbs's methods were worked out in classical mechanics. Why did they keep working when quantum mechanics arrived?

options.label: Quantum mechanics copied them exactly
They were so general that they adapted easily
They ignored the quantum state entirely
They were rewritten from scratch

items.explain: Gibbs's methods were of such generality that they adapted easily to quantum mechanics and still form the foundation of the field.

items.prompt: Maxwell studied what happens when gas molecules collide again and again. What did he argue about temperature?

options.label: Collisions equalize temperatures, so gases tend toward equilibrium
Collisions create hot and cold regions
Collisions stop once gas is at rest
Collisions make all molecules the same speed

items.explain: Maxwell gave the first mechanical argument that molecular collisions equalize temperatures, leading to a tendency toward equilibrium.
